newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan guards against underworld in telecom bid.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan guards against underworld in telecom bid.

text.p: Taiwan will carefully monitor the bidding for its liberalisation of the mobile telephone market to prevent powerful underworld figures from muscling in on lucrative franchises, the justice minister said.

Minister Liao Cheng-hao, in an interview with Reuters, acknowledged that the government was worried about gangsters using kickbacks in an attempt to influence the process under which eight mobile telephone licences will be awarded.

"I cannot rule out such a possibility, and for that reason the ministry will watch the screening process very closely from start to finish to let the gangsters know that they have no way to interfere," Liao said late on Thursday.
"Absolutely no corruption will be allowed," he said.

Seventeen joint ventures, some involving major international telecom firms, have submitted 42 applications for the mobile telephone franchises, which analysts say could yield T$18.7 billion (US$680 million) in sales over the next 10 years.

The Ministry of Transportation and Communication plans to select the winning bidders by the end of 1996, but officials have voiced concerns about potential interference from Taiwan's notoriously powerful gangsters.

Major domestic and foreign firms, including U.S. giants AT&T and Sprint Corp and the influential Koo's Group of Taiwan, are vying for the licences, adding pressure to the need to keep competition clean.

The mobile telephone sector is one of several liberalised by the parliament in January 1996 when it dismantled a decades-old state monopoly by opening them up for private and limited foreign investments.
Gangster involvement in the bidding for major projects has been a constant frustration for Taiwan's government.
Mobsters are said to operate by either ensuring that a certain company wins a bid or by directly joining the bidding and pressuring rivals to back off.
Liao, who became justice minister in a June cabinet reshuffle, said in August he was launching an island-wide campaign to crack down on gangsters.
A police report published in January said Taiwan has 10,582 gangsters and 1,236 gangs.
